hpi:
{{patient_name}} presents with depression, fatigue, weight gain, moon facies, hirsutism, thinning hair, and amenorrhea for six months. This is Cushing disease from a pituitary adenoma — not primary major depressive disorder.

Workup: pregnancy test (amenorrhea); dexamethasone suppression test or 24-hour urine cortisol to confirm hypercortisolism; ACTH level — high ACTH (>20 pg/mL) indicates ACTH-dependent Cushing (pituitary vs ectopic); brain MRI for pituitary tumor when ACTH is elevated.

Definitive treatment is transsphenoidal resection (neurosurgery consult). SSRIs or psychiatry consult alone do not treat the underlying endocrine cause.

case_summary:
Differential: Physiologic hypercortisolism, Adrenal Tumor, Metastatic Disease, Exogenous Cortisol use.

The patient in this case has Cushing Disease. The symptoms the patient is suffering include: weight gain, plethora face (moon face), hirsutism (facial hair growth), thinning hair, and depression. Dexamethasone test is the standard test to test for Cushings syndrome. 24-hour urinary cortisol can also be used.

Once Cushings Syndrome has been established, the cause of it should be determined by measuring ACTH. If ACTH is high (above 20 pg/mL), the syndrome is ACTH-dependent — pituitary tumor, ectopic ACTH, or CRH secretion; obtain brain MRI. If ACTH is low (below 5 pg/mL), evaluate adrenal glands with CT.

In this case ACTH is high (166 pg/mL), pituitary tumor is found on MRI, and neurosurgery should remove the tumor via transsphenoidal microadenomectomy. No points for SSRIs or mental health consult alone — treat the underlying hypercortisolism.
